sections.title: Tutte le strade portano a Roma

units.title: Hello, I'm…
units.fact: Bolzano is bilingual — street signs are in Italian and German — and its museum keeps Ötzi, the 5,300-year-old Iceman.

units.title: Who is who
units.fact: The Council of Trent (1545–63) met here and reshaped the Catholic Church.

units.title: My family
units.fact: Lake Garda is Italy's largest lake; its north end at Riva is a paradise for windsurfers.

units.title: Things and plurals
units.fact: Sirmione's castle rises straight out of Lake Garda; the poet Catullus had a villa at the tip of the peninsula.

units.title: What I do
units.fact: Alessandro Volta, inventor of the battery (and the "volt"), was born in Como.

units.title: Work and the city
units.fact: Milan's cathedral took nearly six centuries to finish and has over 3,400 statues; Leonardo's Last Supper is nearby.

units.title: Questions
units.fact: Bergamo has an upper town (Città Alta) inside Venetian walls, reached by a funicular railway.

units.title: Describing
units.fact: Brescia's Capitolium temple was built by Emperor Vespasian in 73 AD; the Mille Miglia car race starts here.

units.title: Numbers and time
units.fact: Mantua's Ducal Palace has 500 rooms; in Rigoletto, the Duke of Mantua sings "La donna è mobile".

units.title: Seasons in Cremona
units.fact: Stradivari and Guarneri made violins in Cremona; master luthiers still work in its workshops.

units.title: Going and doing
units.fact: Juliet's balcony in Verona is a 20th-century addition — but the Roman Arena (30 AD) still hosts operas.

units.title: Everyday irregulars
units.fact: Andrea Palladio's villas and theater in Vicenza inspired buildings from London to the White House.

units.title: Places and prepositions
units.fact: Padua's university (1222) is one of the oldest in the world; Galileo taught there for 18 years.

units.title: My things
units.fact: Venice is built on 118 islands linked by about 400 bridges; there are no cars at all.

units.title: There is, there are
units.fact: Murano's glassmakers were moved to the island in 1291 to protect Venice from fire — and were forbidden to leave.

units.title: Can, want, must
units.fact: Treviso is the home of tiramisù and Prosecco wine — and of the Benetton fashion brand.

units.title: My day
units.fact: Trieste is Italy's coffee capital: order a "nero" here, not a caffè, and expect fierce winds called the bora.

units.title: What I did
units.fact: Udine's Piazza della Libertà is called "the most beautiful Venetian square on the mainland".

units.title: Where I went
units.fact: Ferrara is Italy's city of bicycles, surrounded by 9 km of Renaissance walls you can ride along.

units.title: Review: mosaics
units.fact: Ravenna's glittering Byzantine mosaics are 1,500 years old; Dante is buried here, exiled from Florence.

units.title: Shopping
units.fact: Turin gave Italy its first capital (1861), its first cars (FIAT) and the gianduja chocolate-hazelnut spread.

units.title: Likes and dislikes
units.fact: Asti's Palio, a bareback horse race through the town, has been run since at least 1275.

units.title: When I was little
units.fact: Alba's white truffles are among the most expensive foods on Earth; Nutella was invented here in 1964.

units.title: Stories of the sea
units.fact: Christopher Columbus was born in Genoa; so was pesto alla genovese.

units.title: Do this!
units.fact: Tiny Portofino has been a harbor since Roman times; its colorful houses are copied in resorts worldwide.

units.title: Plans
units.fact: The five villages of the Cinque Terre were reachable only by sea or footpath until the railway arrived in 1874.

units.title: Some of it, there
units.fact: La Spezia is the gateway to the Cinque Terre and home of the Italian Navy's great arsenal.

units.title: Comparing
units.fact: The Sanremo music festival (since 1951) is Italy's national obsession every February.

units.title: Wishes and politeness
units.fact: Aosta, "the Rome of the Alps", still has its Roman gate and theater; French is co-official in the valley.

units.title: Review: food
units.fact: Parma gives its name to Parmigiano Reggiano and prosciutto di Parma; it is a UNESCO City of Gastronomy.

units.title: Give it to me
units.fact: Bologna's university (1088) is the oldest in continuous operation in the Western world; the city has 40 km of porticoes.

units.title: The thing that…
units.fact: Ferrari, Maserati and balsamic vinegar all come from around Modena; Pavarotti was born here.

units.title: Before that
units.fact: Lucca's Renaissance walls are so wide that the top is a tree-lined park for cycling; Puccini was born here.

units.title: I think that…
units.fact: The Leaning Tower of Pisa began to tilt during construction in 1178; it now leans about 4 degrees.

units.title: Pinocchio
units.fact: Carlo Lorenzini took the pen name Collodi from this Tuscan village; the Pinocchio Park here opened in 1956.

units.title: Art and opinions
units.fact: Florence was the cradle of the Renaissance; Dante's Florentine became the basis of modern Italian.

units.title: Doubts and hopes
units.fact: From the hill of Fiesole, older than Florence itself, you see the whole city below.

units.title: If I were…
units.fact: Siena's Palio horse race lasts about 90 seconds and is run around the shell-shaped Piazza del Campo.

units.title: What's happening now
units.fact: San Gimignano still has 14 of its 72 medieval tower-houses — a skyline of status symbols.

units.title: Review: the wine town
units.fact: Montepulciano's Vino Nobile has been praised since 1685, when a poet called it "king of all wines".

units.title: How it's done
units.fact: Arezzo's frescoes by Piero della Francesca and its huge monthly antiques fair draw visitors from everywhere.

units.title: Some, any, none
units.fact: Cortona is one of the oldest towns in Tuscany, founded by the Etruscans.

units.title: Little words, big words
units.fact: Perugia makes the Baci chocolates — each wrapped with a love note — and hosts a chocolate festival.

units.title: Saints and old texts
units.fact: St. Francis of Assisi wrote the "Canticle of the Creatures", one of the first poems in Italian.

units.title: Festival of two worlds
units.fact: Spoleto's Festival dei Due Mondi has brought opera, theater and dance to its piazzas every summer since 1958.

units.title: Underground city
units.fact: Orvieto sits on a cliff of volcanic tuff riddled with over 1,000 caves, wells and tunnels.

units.title: The ideal city
units.fact: Urbino was Raphael's birthplace and a model of the Renaissance "ideal city".

units.title: Ports and trade
units.fact: Ancona's name comes from the Greek for "elbow", after the curve of its coast.

units.title: Legends
units.fact: Legend says angels carried the Holy House of Nazareth to Loreto in 1294.

units.title: Review: rebuilding
units.fact: L'Aquila, badly damaged by the 2009 earthquake, has been carefully rebuilt; it has "99" fountains, squares and churches by legend.

units.title: Popes and baths
units.fact: Viterbo was a papal city: the longest conclave in history (1268–71) happened here.

units.title: Gardens and fountains
units.fact: Villa d'Este at Tivoli has hundreds of fountains, including one that once played music with water.

units.title: The Colosseum
units.fact: The Colosseum (80 AD) held about 50,000 spectators; its floor could be flooded for mock sea battles.

units.title: Neighborhood life
units.fact: Trastevere, "across the Tiber", is Rome's old working-class quarter of cobbles, ivy and trattorie.

units.title: Faith and power
units.fact: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world; the Swiss Guard has protected the Pope since 1506.

units.title: Out of town
units.fact: Romans escape to the Castelli Romani hills for porchetta and Frascati white wine.

units.title: Roman daily life
units.fact: Ostia Antica was Rome's port: its ruins include a public toilet with seats for 20.

units.title: From marsh to farmland
units.fact: The Pontine Marshes south of Rome were drained in the 1930s; Latina was founded on the reclaimed land.

units.title: Seaside
units.fact: Gaeta's "Montagna Spaccata" is a mountain split by a cleft, said to have cracked at the death of Christ.

units.title: War and peace
units.fact: Montecassino abbey, founded by St. Benedict in 529, was destroyed in 1944 and rebuilt.

units.title: Conversation and gestures
units.fact: Pizza Margherita was named in 1889 for Queen Margherita; Neapolitan pizza-making is UNESCO heritage.

units.title: A frozen moment
units.fact: Pompeii was buried by Vesuvius in 79 AD; its graffiti still show election slogans and jokes.

units.title: Ancient papyri
units.fact: At Herculaneum a whole library of carbonized scrolls was found; scientists are now reading them with X-rays.

units.title: Danger and nature
units.fact: Vesuvius is the only active volcano on mainland Europe; about 600,000 people live in its red zone.

units.title: Lemons and songs
units.fact: Sorrento's lemons become limoncello; the song "Torna a Surriento" was written here in 1902.

units.title: Island life
units.fact: Capri's Blue Grotto glows because sunlight enters through an underwater opening.

units.title: Fashion and style
units.fact: Positano's cliffside houses inspired a whole style of beach fashion in the 1950s.

units.title: Old maritime power
units.fact: Amalfi was a maritime republic rivaling Venice and Genoa; it still makes handmade paper.

units.title: Medicine
units.fact: The Schola Medica Salernitana was Europe's first medical school, already famous around the year 1000.

units.title: Review: Greek temples
units.fact: Paestum's Greek temples (6th–5th century BC) are better preserved than many in Greece itself.

units.title: Life in the stone
units.fact: Matera's Sassi cave dwellings have been inhabited for some 9,000 years; it was European Capital of Culture in 2019.

units.title: The trulli
units.fact: The trulli of Alberobello have cone-shaped dry-stone roofs, once built so they could be dismantled before tax inspections.

units.title: Saint Nicholas
units.fact: The relics of St. Nicholas — the original Santa Claus — were brought to Bari by sailors in 1087.

units.title: The Florence of the South
units.fact: Lecce's soft local limestone allowed its Baroque churches to be carved like lace.

units.title: East meets west
units.fact: Otranto is Italy's easternmost town; on clear days you can see Albania across the sea.

units.title: Sea and myth
units.fact: Taranto was founded by Spartans in 706 BC; the tarantella dance and the tarantula are named after it.

units.title: Books and learning
units.fact: Legend says the Visigoth king Alaric is buried with his treasure beneath the rivers of Cosenza.

units.title: Red onions and sunsets
units.fact: Tropea's red onions are so sweet that you can even find red-onion ice cream in town.

units.title: The bronze warriors
units.fact: The Riace Bronzes, two Greek warriors found by a diver in 1972, are the pride of Reggio's museum.

units.title: Monsters of the strait
units.fact: Scylla, the six-headed monster of Homer's Odyssey, was said to lurk in the rocks of this fishing village.

units.title: Crossing the strait
units.fact: Messina's cathedral has one of the world's largest astronomical clocks, with a golden lion that roars at noon.

units.title: Theater with a view
units.fact: Taormina's Greek theater looks out over the sea to smoking Mount Etna.

units.title: Living with Etna
units.fact: Catania has been rebuilt many times after Etna's eruptions; its elephant statue is made of lava.

units.title: Greeks and inventors
units.fact: Archimedes lived in Syracuse and supposedly shouted "Eureka!" in his bath.

units.title: Rebuilt after the earthquake
units.fact: After the 1693 earthquake, Ragusa and its neighbors were rebuilt in a glorious late Baroque style.

units.title: The valley of temples
units.fact: Agrigento's Valley of the Temples holds some of the best-preserved Greek temples anywhere.

units.title: Markets and mixtures
units.fact: Palermo's markets echo its Arab, Norman and Spanish past; try arancine and cannoli.

units.title: Golden mosaics
units.fact: Monreale Cathedral's mosaics cover about 6,400 square meters with gold.

units.title: Sardinia
units.fact: Pink flamingos live in the lagoons of Cagliari, right next to the city.

units.title: The journey's end
units.fact: In Alghero people still speak a form of Catalan; your Grand Tour ends at the sea. Bravo!
